questions.topic: Stale transaction data after Angular navigation
questions.question: A transaction list shows stale data after navigation. How would you identify the cause?

definition.text: Stale views display outdated information after navigation or refresh.

motivation.whyIntroduced: Navigation reuses browser processes, services and potentially components; earlier responses or cached state can outlive the screen that requested them. Financial history must not silently present outdated transactions as current. Diagnose the responsible layer before modifying change detection.
motivation.historicalNote: Client-side routing makes navigation faster than full page reloads, but also requires explicit decisions about data freshness and request lifetimes. Reusable services and caching increase the need for invalidation strategies.

problemSolved.before: A user navigates from account A to B while A’s slow HTTP response is still in flight; the component displays A’s rows under B’s heading.
problemSolved.after: Observe route-parameter changes, request new data for the active account, cancel or ignore outdated responses and key caches by authorized identity and account. Render explicit loading, error and freshness states.
benefits: Prevent account A results appearing under B.
Make stale response races reproducible.
Keep component rendering separate from server authorization and cache invalidation.
Give users a trustworthy indication when history was last refreshed.

characteristics: Route changes can occur while an HTTP request is still pending.
switchMap cancels an obsolete HTTP subscription, but cancellation does not undo completed server work.
Cache identity must include account and user/tenant scope, not merely endpoint path.
AsyncPipe subscribes and unsubscribes automatically when its view is destroyed.
The backend must independently authorize account access even if the UI filters account choices.

simpleAnalogy.title: Restaurant orders
simpleAnalogy.explanation: A waiter must deliver a meal to the table that placed the order, not whichever table most recently spoke. The receipt and table number must travel with the request.

industryExample.scenario: A fictional customer switches rapidly between two accounts while viewing the last 30 transactions; responses arrive in the reverse order.
industryExample.implementation: Route paramMap is mapped to a distinct account ID; switchMap issues GET /api/accounts/:id/transactions, and the template reads one observable view state. Backend checks account ownership on every request.
industryExample.businessImpact: Prevents misleading financial history and cross-account data display; a visible refresh timestamp makes data age explicit.
constraints: Never interpret client-side filtering as authorization.
User-specific caches must be cleared or partitioned across sign-out/sign-in.
No stale value should be portrayed as current during a network failure.

useCases: Route-driven API search or detail screens.

steps: Read the active route account ID.
Mark view state loading for the new ID.
Cancel the previous subscription when another ID arrives.
Request authorized transaction history for the newest account.
Render success or error only for the active request.
Verify through an intentionally delayed-response test.

diagrams.mermaid:
sequenceDiagram

  participant Router as Angular Router
  participant View as Transactions Component
  participant API as Authorized Account API
  Customer->>Router: Navigate Account A then B
  Router->>View: paramMap emits A
  View->>API: GET A transactions
  Router->>View: paramMap emits B
  View--xAPI: Unsubscribe obsolete A request
  View->>API: GET B transactions
  API-->>View: B rows
  View-->>Customer: Show only B transactions
diagrams.caption: Illustrative banking flow using fictional accounts. Authorization, identity boundaries and financial correctness are enforced on the server.

codeExample.runtime: Angular standalone routed component using RxJS and HttpClient; configure an authorized API and HttpClient in the consuming application.
codeExample.explanation: switchMap replaces the previous account request whenever the route parameter changes; AsyncPipe manages the subscription. A loading state belongs to the current account. On a real banking screen, use masked account labels, transaction dates and appropriate error logging.

projectExperience.example: For a fictional banking portal, I would throttle the network, switch accounts A→B→A and record whether delayed responses ever contaminate the visible account list.
evidenceToCollect: Network recording showing overlapping account requests.
Automated test with delayed A and immediate B responses.
Screenshots showing correct account labels and error state.
projectExperience.doNotClaim: Portfolio implementation is proposed, not verified employment or completed professional experience. Substitute truthful project evidence only after execution.

pitfalls: Assuming the router always destroys a component on parameter-only navigation.
Using mergeMap for replace-latest account selection, permitting stale responses.
Maintaining a global unscoped transaction array across multiple authenticated identities.
Mistaking an OnPush issue for a race without checking network timing.
Caching under a constant key that omits account identity.
whenNotToUse: Do not store or return another customer’s transactions from a client-side filter.
Do not use switchMap blindly for payment writes: unsubscribing from a client request does not safely cancel a transfer.
Do not show cached data as current without explicit age or freshness semantics.

alternatives.name: switchMap route-driven request
alternatives.bestFor: Latest selected account replaces prior read
alternatives.tradeoff: Cancels old subscriptions; account request validation remains on server.

alternatives.name: Resolver with router-managed data
alternatives.bestFor: Navigation that requires data before activation
alternatives.tradeoff: Can delay navigation and needs refresh strategy.

alternatives.name: Scoped query cache
alternatives.bestFor: Repeated account visits with controlled freshness
alternatives.tradeoff: Requires identity-aware cache keys, invalidation and disclosure of stale data.

testing.strategy: Use HttpTestingController to hold the A response, navigate to B, flush B and verify only B renders. Add a cache-isolation and sign-out test. Use browser DevTools to correlate route, request URL, response and render time.

testCases.expected: B account title and B transactions render even if A was requested first.
No duplicate read when accountId has not changed.
An error state appears without account details.
An explicit empty state appears.

negativeCases: Deliver a delayed A response after B navigates and assert A cannot overwrite B.
Switch identity and assert no prior-user transactions remain visible.
testing.verificationCommand: ng test && ng build; browser network throttle with rapid account switching

questions.topic: Cross-functional delivery ownership for a banking dashboard
questions.question: How would you divide banking dashboard development among frontend and backend engineers?

definition.text: Clear ownership lets teams deliver dependable banking features together.

motivation.whyIntroduced: UI work depends on domain semantics, API contracts and secure data access. When ownership is unclear, developers build incompatible models or assume validation is handled elsewhere. A thin vertical slice clarifies handoffs before large parallel implementation.
motivation.historicalNote: Cross-functional feature teams emerged to reduce handoff delays between siloed UI, API, database and testing disciplines. Banking adds risk, audit and regulatory stakeholders whose work cannot be left to the final release.

problemSolved.before: Frontend engineers invent an available-balance formula while the API team returns posted-only balances; QA receives inconsistent definitions and release quality suffers.
problemSolved.after: Agree an explicit account-summary contract, ownership boundaries, acceptance criteria, and one end-to-end slice before splitting parallel dashboard, history and notifications work.
benefits: Avoid contradictory definitions of available versus posted balance.
Expose missing authorization and audit requirements before coding.
Enable parallel delivery via agreed interfaces.
Make tests and release evidence part of normal ownership.

characteristics: One product owner owns user behavior and acceptance outcomes.
Frontend owns accessibility, presentation and client state—not authoritative banking rules.
Backend owns authorization and consistent account read models.
QA and security collaborate on cross-cutting failure cases.
API schemas, example fixtures and trace identifiers form shared integration contracts.

simpleAnalogy.title: Building a bridge
simpleAnalogy.explanation: One team handles the span and another the supports; they need the same plans and a joint load test or the pieces cannot meet safely.

industryExample.scenario: A banking organization introduces a dashboard for current and savings accounts and needs frontend, backend, QA, risk and product coordination.
industryExample.implementation: Lead a contract workshop, assign accountable owners by deliverable and deploy one authenticated account-summary vertical slice before parallelizing transactions and alerts.
industryExample.businessImpact: Fewer late integration surprises, clear quality ownership and faster incident resolution.
constraints: Identity and account authorization remain enforced server-side.
Money fields need currency and minor-unit precision rules documented.
Audit requirements are agreed with compliance stakeholders, not inferred by UI developers.

useCases: Agreeing API contracts before parallel work.

steps: Gather acceptance criteria for display and error states.
Define OpenAPI DTO and examples.
Assign frontend, backend, QA and security responsibilities.
Build authenticated account-summary vertical slice.
Test forbidden accounts, pending holds and stale responses.
Release behind a feature flag with monitoring and rollback.

codeExample.explanation: The DTO defines account and currency semantics in one place. Its validator is intentionally basic and does not replace runtime DTO validation on either side. The team should test the generated client contract against actual API responses.

projectExperience.example: In the portfolio project I would record API contract decisions, assign ownership for each widget and demonstrate one authenticated dashboard slice with a joint test.
evidenceToCollect: OpenAPI file with sample response and 401/403 cases.

projectExperience.doNotClaim: Portfolio implementation is proposed, not verified employment or completed professional experience. Substitute truthful project evidence only after execution.

pitfalls: Assigning risk review only after an implementation is finished.
Treating frontend validation as a substitute for server ownership.
Defining only successful API responses and ignoring error semantics.
Writing independently maintained DTOs without compatibility checks.
whenNotToUse: Do not let the client compute authoritative account balances.
Do not split ownership so every cross-team defect has no accountable resolver.
Do not bypass account authorization to unblock a frontend demo.

alternatives.name: Layer-aligned teams
alternatives.tradeoff: Greater handoff and release coordination needs.

alternatives.name: Backend-for-frontend team
alternatives.tradeoff: Extra service boundary and ownership costs.

testing.strategy: Require API contract tests, Angular accessibility/fixture tests, backend authorization checks, E2E happy and failure paths and a release rollback rehearsal.

testCases.expected: Frontend mock matches server response shape and status expectations.
Backend denies access and frontend renders safe failure state.
Contract compatibility checks detect incompatible response changes.
Flag and rollback allow controlled activation.

negativeCases: API field renamed without a version or compatibility rule.
Banking domain owner changes available-balance definition after build: ensure contract and tests are updated together.
testing.verificationCommand: npm test && npm run build; execute OpenAPI contract and E2E checks in CI

questions.topic: Review standards for accurate and secure financial data display
questions.question: What coding and review standards should your team apply to financial data displays?

definition.text: Financial display standards prevent misleading amounts and sensitive leaks.

motivation.whyIntroduced: Currency values and sensitive identifiers must be consistently displayed across many screens. A small formatting mistake, stale snapshot or incorrect sign can be misconstrued as a money movement. Standards make these concerns reviewable and testable.
motivation.historicalNote: Financial institutions use internal control standards to reduce operational and customer-facing errors. Modern frontend code review translates domain rules into reusable components, fixtures, automated checks and explicit ownership.

problemSolved.before: A developer formats all currencies to two decimals, shows unmasked identifiers in logs and labels a pending item as posted.
problemSolved.after: Adopt a review checklist covering money models, currency decimals, balance semantics, masking, accessibility, precision, authorization, errors and sensitive-data telemetry.
benefits: Currency formatting follows the correct ISO currency precision.
Values are labeled by status and never guessed from missing data.
Sensitive identifiers are masked, and logs contain no raw financial details.
Automated tests guard financial representation and negative cases.

characteristics: Separate amounts and currencies in typed models.
Use locale/currency-aware formatting rather than hardcoded decimal assumptions.
Label available, posted and pending amounts explicitly.
Mask sensitive identifiers according to product policy; masking is not authorization.
Review accessibility, freshness and both success and error presentations.

simpleAnalogy.title: Medical prescription label
simpleAnalogy.explanation: A prescription must use the right units and patient details; a small formatting mistake can be consequential. Money labels deserve similar disciplined review.

industryExample.scenario: A banking app supports INR and JPY account cards. A developer divides all minor units by 100 before formatting, incorrectly displaying Japanese yen amounts.
industryExample.implementation: Keep amount data as integer minor units with explicit currency; a shared presentation function determines fractional digits for the currency and formats using Intl.NumberFormat. Reconciliation remains backend-owned.
industryExample.businessImpact: Prevents misleading balances and currency mix-ups; shared fixtures make regressions visible early.
constraints: Avoid JavaScript floating-point arithmetic for authoritative money movement.
This formatter is for display only; use backend-approved money libraries for financial calculations.
Privacy and masking rules depend on account type and local policy.

steps: Backend returns amountMinor, ISO currency and asOf.
Client parses an authorized response with runtime validation.
Shared display helper determines currency digits.
Angular renders labeled values, masks identifiers and exposes freshness.
Unit tests cover INR, JPY, zero, negatives and missing currency.
Review and CI block unsafe changes.

  UI-->>CI: Rendered labels and snapshot tests
  CI-->>UI: Pass or require correction

codeExample.runtime: Framework-independent TypeScript display formatter used by Angular presentation components; standard Intl implementation is provided by the JavaScript runtime.
codeExample.explanation: The formatter queries the locale currency fraction-digit defaults rather than dividing every amount by 100. It validates safe integer input and explicitly limits the calculation to display-only situations, not accounting.

projectExperience.example: In the portfolio banking UI I would add a shared money-display utility and require PR reviewers to check currencies, masking, negative values, empty states and accessibility.
evidenceToCollect: Unit tests for INR and JPY display with known values.
Review checklist signed off on posted/available labels and masking.
CI evidence for invalid/negative and very large values.

pitfalls: Hardcoding currency to INR when account response is multi-currency.
Converting arbitrary precision ledger decimals to floats for calculations.
Logging raw account or transfer identifiers.
Rendering an unavailable value as zero.
Assuming displaying a masked account number prevents backend access.
whenNotToUse: Do not use formatted display strings as the source of truth for any transfer.
Do not mix distinct currencies in a total without an explicit FX rule.
Do not assume a fixed two-decimal currency representation worldwide.

alternatives.name: Shared display component
alternatives.bestFor: Standard labels and accessibility across pages
alternatives.tradeoff: Needs versioned contracts and careful review.

testing.strategy: Run unit tests across supported currencies/locales, accessibility assertions and permission tests. Use code review checklists for money precision, status labels, privacy and fallback states.

testCases.expected: 12345 minor units format as ₹123.45 under en-IN.
12345 minor units format as ¥12,345 under ja-JP.
Unsafe/non-integer amount is rejected.
UI displays unavailable, not a fabricated zero.

negativeCases: Unexpected currency code causes formatter failure: recover safely without leaking internals.
Very large integer threatens double precision: ensure backend and display contract avoid unsafe conversion.

questions.question: Your team discovers a bug where a transaction amount displays with the wrong currency. How should the defect be handled?

definition.text: Currency display defects require containment, correction, and verified recovery.

motivation.whyIntroduced: An amount shown in the wrong currency can cause customer misunderstanding and undermine trust. Financial severity depends on whether only presentation is wrong or money posting, exchange-rate conversion or downstream records are affected. The first step is to establish scope and contain user impact.
motivation.historicalNote: Incident response practices separate urgent containment from root-cause remediation. A display bug can be low-code but high-impact in customer-facing financial systems.

problemSolved.before: A UI shows ₹5,000 for an account denominated in USD and the team treats it as a minor visual inconsistency.
problemSolved.after: Open an incident, identify impacted screens/accounts, distinguish display from ledger correctness, disable affected presentation if needed, fix contract/formatter, test all relevant currencies and monitor rollout.
benefits: Rapidly reduce customer exposure to misleading financial information.
Determine whether transactions or only display were affected.
Establish reproducible fixtures and owners.
Prevent recurrence through contract tests and release controls.

characteristics: Assess customer harm and incident severity before prioritizing cosmetic polish.
Verify server-side currency and minor unit values before blaming rendering.
Coordinate product, support, security and operations as appropriate.
Prefer reversible mitigation and tested rollback over an unreviewed hotfix.
Capture timeline and root-cause evidence without logging financial secrets.

simpleAnalogy.title: Wrong measurement unit
simpleAnalogy.explanation: A weather report showing 20°F as 20°C is misleading even if the underlying sensor recorded a correct value. First check the sensor, then the unit label and conversion.

industryExample.scenario: A banking release displays an INR currency symbol on USD-denominated transaction rows in the activity list for one locale.
industryExample.implementation: Compare API DTO and raw currency fields with formatted UI output, isolate an incorrect default in a shared formatting component, deploy verified fix behind controls and verify no ledger or FX processing was altered.
industryExample.businessImpact: Protects customer decision-making and gives the business a defensible record of cause, scope and recovery.
constraints: Never infer the source currency from the user locale.
Do not change ledger amounts or exchange rates to compensate for a presentation bug.
Contact and disclosure decisions follow actual organizational and jurisdictional processes.

steps: Alert detected via user report or monitoring.
Incident lead assigns severity and records affected versions and accounts.
Trace displayed record to API currency and server-of-record currency.
Mitigate with rollback or feature flag if necessary.
Fix formatting and add contract/unit/E2E regression tests.
Release gradually, monitor and document post-incident actions.

pitfalls: Assuming all currency symbols are unambiguous.
Changing stored amounts to match a mistaken UI label.
Skipping impact analysis because the issue appears cosmetic.
Using locale as the authoritative transaction currency.
Issuing an immediate hotfix without focused tests or rollback.
whenNotToUse: Do not change backend ledger balance values to conceal a UI defect.
Do not send customer PII or access tokens in incident tickets or logs.
Do not close the incident before customer-facing recovery is verified.

testing.strategy: Verify raw server currency independently from UI format, add tests for locale variation and fractional digits, run end-to-end checks after rollout and document an incident RCA.

testCases.expected: Still identifies USD rather than becoming INR.
Shows zero-decimal style under supported locale.
Previously known safe release displays approved amount labels.
Incident timeline and validated source fields are retained securely.

negativeCases: Service returns an unsupported currency; avoid silently substituting the customer locale currency.
Mixed currency batch rendered with a single default currency; reject or label each row correctly.

questions.topic: Frontend and backend responsibility boundaries in banking
questions.question: What responsibilities should belong to the Angular application versus the banking backend?

definition.text: Angular presents interactions; banking backends enforce authoritative business rules.

motivation.whyIntroduced: Browser code executes on devices controlled by users, so it cannot be trusted to enforce financial rules or access permissions. A clear boundary allows Angular to optimize interaction while server services apply identity, authorization, ledger consistency and audit requirements.
motivation.historicalNote: Thick-client and thin-client designs have long debated where business logic belongs. Modern SPAs provide rich browser experiences, but security and integrity decisions still require trusted server-side enforcement.

problemSolved.before: The Angular application chooses the transferable amount, computes an account balance locally and relies on hidden buttons to stop unauthorized transfers.
problemSolved.after: Angular handles forms, accessibility, display, UX-oriented checks and safe request composition; backend validates user identity, account ownership, limits, balances, idempotency, ledger updates and audit records.
benefits: Server rules remain enforceable even with malicious or modified clients.
UI can provide immediate feedback without becoming financial truth.
API contracts let web and mobile clients share authoritative logic.
Testing can separate presentation behavior from monetary guarantees.

characteristics: The frontend can validate for user experience, but backend must validate independently.
Route guards and hidden actions are not authorization controls.
The backend owns balances, limits, transaction status and durable effects.
The browser may cache authorized read-only views with explicit freshness rules.
Audit records and secure identities must not rely on client-reported claims.

simpleAnalogy.title: Airport check-in
simpleAnalogy.explanation: A kiosk checks that fields are filled in and helps choose a seat, but airport systems authorize tickets and enforce whether boarding is permitted.

industryExample.scenario: A customer enters a simulated transfer between two accounts. The frontend validates presence and format; the backend verifies ownership, available funds and transfer constraints and produces a transfer reference.
industryExample.implementation: Angular posts a transfer request DTO; NestJS controller performs schema checks, authorization and uses an application service to call a simulated transfer processor. In real banking, balances and posting require a transactional ledger/integration, not a naive two-row update.
industryExample.businessImpact: Protects integrity and enables consistent rules across mobile, web and partner channels.
constraints: A demo endpoint must not be presented as production-grade payment processing.
Idempotency must be enforced durably server-side for retryable transfer requests.
Balance correctness can depend on external banking networks and clearing states.

useCases: Separating client UX validation from backend enforcement.
Planning financial audit and trust boundaries.

steps: Angular validates form interaction and submits request.
Backend authenticates requester using secure session or token.
Backend authorizes source account and validates destination/limits.
Transfer application service uses durable idempotency and ledger/payment integration.
Backend records auditable result and returns a stable reference.
Angular displays the confirmed or pending status without inventing success.

sequenceDiagram

  participant UI as Angular Transfer Form

codeExample.runtime: TypeScript DTO and frontend form-validation helper for an Angular banking simulation; a secure backend and durable transfer processor must be implemented separately.
codeExample.explanation: The code models what the client can check locally and explicitly identifies what it cannot prove. The backend must never trust a user-provided sourceAccountId or amount merely because TypeScript types and Angular validation accepted them.

projectExperience.example: In a fictional banking portal I would document trust boundaries and simulate positive/negative transfers, then show server rejections even after bypassing browser validation.
evidenceToCollect: Backend tests showing forbidden accounts and invalid amounts are rejected.
Demonstration that changing the browser request cannot bypass backend rules.
projectExperience.doNotClaim: Portfolio implementation is proposed, not verified employment or completed professional experience. Substitute truthful project evidence only after execution.

pitfalls: Treating a route guard as sufficient access control.
Assuming TypeScript interfaces validate incoming JSON at runtime.
Updating balances in Angular as if client success creates settled money.
Retrying non-idempotent transfer POST requests automatically.
Trusting sourceAccountId without matching it to authenticated principal.
whenNotToUse: Never place ledger posting or authorization guarantees in the browser.
Never mark a transfer settled before the backend confirms its real status.
Never store secrets or protected bank credentials in delivered frontend code.

alternatives.name: Angular UI plus trusted API
alternatives.tradeoff: Requires clear contracts and network failure handling.

alternatives.name: Backend-for-frontend facade
alternatives.bestFor: UI aggregating multiple banking read models

alternatives.name: Server-rendered read-only page
alternatives.tradeoff: May provide a less interactive workflow without client enhancements.

testing.strategy: Use client unit tests only for UX feedback; backend integration tests for authorization/validation/idempotency; E2E tests for real response statuses; threat-model browser request manipulation.

testCases.expected: Angular blocks clearly invalid form submission for usability.
Server returns forbidden despite browser manipulation.
Server processing returns one logical result and does not double-post.
UI shows pending, not confirmed.
UI does not show false success or decrement authoritative balance.

negativeCases: Replay the same idempotency key with conflicting payload; backend must reject or safely handle conflict according to contract.
Retry after network timeout while server may have completed; query durable transfer state rather than assuming failure.
testing.verificationCommand: ng test && ng build; run API authorization, idempotency and failure-injection integration tests
